section.title: Return to the LORD
section.sectionRationale: This is the hinge of the whole book. After the terror of the advancing army, God interrupts with two words, yet even now, and swings the door of mercy wide open. The call is not to a religion of torn clothes but of torn hearts, grounded in the ancient revelation of God as gracious and compassionate.
section.thesis: Even at the edge of judgment God calls His people to return with all their heart, because He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, and relents from disaster, so genuine, whole-hearted repentance is met by a God eager to forgive.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the divine invitation, yet even now return to Me; the ground of hope, rend your hearts because God is gracious and may relent; and the summons to a solemn assembly where priests plead for the people.

units.label: Yet even now, return to Me

verses.text: “Yet even now,” declares the LORD, “{{shuv|return}} to Me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning.”

So rend your {{lev|hearts}} and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God. For He is {{channun|gracious}} and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. And He relents from sending disaster.
Who knows? He may turn and relent and leave a blessing behind Him, grain and drink offerings for the LORD your God.
Blow the {{shofar|ram’s horn}} in Zion, consecrate a fast, proclaim a sacred assembly.
Gather the people, sanctify the congregation, assemble the aged, gather the children, even those nursing at the breast. Let the bridegroom leave his room, and the bride her chamber.

units.label: The priests plead: spare Your people
units.note: why should they say, where is their God?

verses.text: Let the priests who minister before the LORD weep between the portico and the altar, saying, “Spare Your people, O LORD, and do not make Your heritage a reproach, an object of scorn among the nations. Why should they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’”

shofar.gloss: A ram's horn trumpet, blown to summon assemblies and mark sacred moments. In chapter two the same horn sounded the alarm of war; here it calls the people together to a holy fast and solemn assembly. The instrument of dread becomes the instrument of gathering, rallying the whole community to seek God.

shuv.gloss: To turn, to return, to come back. It is the great prophetic word for repentance, picturing a change of direction, turning from sin and turning back to God. Joel uses it twice in these verses, and the return he calls for is not outward ritual but a turning of the whole heart back to the LORD who is waiting to receive it.

lev.gloss: The heart, the inner core of a person, the seat of thought, will, and affection, not merely emotion. To rend the heart rather than the garments is to let the inner life, not just the outward show, be broken open before God. Joel insists that true repentance reaches the center of a person, where God alone sees.

channun.gloss: Gracious, disposed to show unmerited favor to the needy and undeserving. It heads the ancient self-revelation of God from Exodus 34, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. Joel grounds the call to return not in the people's worthiness but in God's own gracious character, which is the only sure basis for hope.

basic.context: After eleven verses of gathering darkness, God suddenly breaks in with two words: yet even now. However late it is, the door to return is still open. The call is to come back to God with the whole heart, not just to tear clothes in a show of grief but to let the heart itself be broken. Priests are to lead the whole community, young and old, in pleading for mercy.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the turning point of the book, and its hope rests entirely on the character of God, quoted from Exodus 34: gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in love. Joel is not teaching that repentance earns forgiveness; he is teaching that a merciful God invites sinners to return and may relent. The cautious who knows keeps it from being presumption while holding the door open.
basic.originalLanguages: The key word is shuv, to turn or return, the great prophetic word for repentance, and Joel uses it twice. God wants the heart, the lev, rent open, not the garments. And the hope rests on God being channun, gracious, the first word of His great self-description in Exodus 34.
basic.typology: The priests weeping between the portico and the altar, pleading spare Your people, foreshadow the greater High Priest, Jesus, who intercedes for His people. The relenting God who leaves a blessing behind Him points to the God who in Christ turns from wrath to blessing for all who return. The torn heart anticipates the new heart God promises to give.
basic.christ: The call to rend the heart exposes that we cannot truly change our own hearts, which is why God promised to give a new heart and put His Spirit within, fulfilled in Christ. Jesus is the true and greater priest who does not merely plead spare Your people but secures their sparing by taking the disaster on Himself. Because He bore the judgment, the God who relents can pour blessing behind Him.
basic.god: This is the clearest window in Joel onto the heart of God: gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, overflowing with loving devotion, and ready to relent from disaster when His people return. His justice in the preceding verses and His mercy here are not in conflict; the same holy God who warns is the God who longs to forgive. He does not wait for us to clean ourselves up but calls us back as we are.
basic.crossReferences: The description of God is lifted from Exodus 34:6-7. Ezekiel 36 promises the new heart that this passage exposes our need for. Psalm 51 models the broken and contrite heart God will not despise, and Luke 15 shows the father running to the returning son.
basic.oneStory: Yet even now is the gospel in miniature, God opening the way home to sinners at the last hour. It runs from Exodus 34 through the prophets to the cross, where the God who relents from disaster does so justly because Christ bore it, and on to the Father who still runs to welcome all who return.

context.literary:
The unit is a single movement of speech, and the grammar carries it. Verses 12 to 14 are first person divine speech that slides into the prophet's own voice, so that 'declares the LORD' in verse 12 gives way to 'the LORD your God' in verse 13. Then come seven imperatives in verses 15 and 16, blow, consecrate, proclaim, gather, sanctify, assemble, gather again, and the unit ends with a prayer that the priests are told to pray, verse 17. God invites, the prophet organises, the priests plead. The whole nation is being walked from the throne room to the altar.

The pivot word is gam attah, 'yet even now,' and it answers the previous unit exactly. Chapter 2 verses 1 to 11 ended with a rhetorical question about who can endure the day. Verse 12 answers it with the only reply the book offers: no one can endure it, so return. Notice the doubled use of shuv in verses 12 and 13 and its third appearance in verse 14, where the same verb is used of God. The people are to turn, and God 'may turn.' The unit is built on the hope that two turnings will meet.

The call also reuses vocabulary from the first chapter. 'Consecrate a fast, proclaim a sacred assembly' in verse 15 repeats the summons of Joel 1:14, and the ram's horn that sounded an alarm in Joel 2:1 is blown again, now to gather worshippers rather than to warn of an army. The same instruments and words that announced the crisis are turned into the means of meeting God in it. The reversal is deliberate, and it prepares the ground for the answer that begins in verse 18.

The grammar of verse 14 is worth slowing for. 'Who knows' opens a question that never states its answer, and the clause that follows is a chain of three verbs, turn, relent, leave a blessing. The sentence ends not with rain or harvest but with 'grain and drink offerings for the LORD your God,' the very offerings that Joel 1:9 and 1:13 said were cut off from the temple. The blessing God may leave behind is first of all the restored ability to worship.
context.historical:
Joel gives no king's name and no date, and the book's setting is argued over, but this passage assumes a functioning temple, a serving priesthood and a community that knows how to fast and lament together. The elders and priests carry the weight of leadership here, which fits either the years before the exile or the generations after the return. What matters for reading is the world of practice behind the words.

Tearing clothes was the ordinary sign of grief and horror, as when Jacob learned of Joseph, Genesis 37:34, or Joshua prayed after the defeat at Ai, Joshua 7:6, or Ezra heard of intermarriage, Ezra 9:3 to 5. It was visible, quick and cheap. The prophets repeatedly warned that such displays could be empty, Isaiah 58:5 to 7 and Hosea 6:1 to 6 among them. Joel does not abolish the fast, he commands it in the same breath, but he insists that the tearing happen where no one can see it.

The call to leave nothing out is startling in its details. Deuteronomy 24:5 exempted a newly married man from war and public duty for a year so he could bring joy to his wife. Joel summons the bridegroom from his room and the bride from her chamber, which means even that exemption yields to the emergency. The nursing infant, who cannot repent, is brought as well. This is the whole covenant community standing together under the threat, in the way Nineveh's whole population fasted in Jonah 3:5 to 9.

The priests are stationed 'between the portico and the altar,' that is, in the open court in front of the temple building, the place where sacrifices were offered, 2 Chronicles 8:12. The same spot appears in Ezekiel 8:16, where twenty-five men stand there with their backs to the temple, bowing to the sun. Joel's priests stand there facing the sanctuary, weeping, which makes the place a picture of right worship against wrong. The prayer they are given was a recognisable form: Moses had pleaded that Egypt would say God destroyed His people, Exodus 32:12, and the psalmists asked 'Where is their God?' on Israel's behalf, Psalm 79:10 and Psalm 115:2.
context.canonical:
Verse 13 is one of the most quoted sentences in the Old Testament. Its source is the self-disclosure at Sinai after the golden calf, when God proclaimed His own name to Moses, Exodus 34:6 to 7. That line is then picked up as the people's creed in Numbers 14:18, Nehemiah 9:17, Psalm 86:15, Psalm 103:8 and Psalm 145:8. Joel adds his own phrase, 'and He relents from sending disaster,' in place of the Exodus reference to faithfulness and truth, and he puts 'gracious' ahead of 'compassionate.' Jonah quotes the same words in Jonah 4:2, resentfully, as the reason he ran from Nineveh. What Joel offers as an invitation, Jonah treats as a scandal.

The call to turn with the whole heart belongs to a long strand of Deuteronomic and prophetic teaching. Deuteronomy 30:2 to 6 foresees an exiled Israel returning 'with all your heart and all your soul,' and then promises that God Himself will circumcise their hearts. Jeremiah 4:1 to 4 joins the two ideas Joel joins, return and heart circumcision. The paradox of the command and the gift is therefore already old when Joel preaches it, and it is resolved in the new covenant promises of Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26 to 27.

The prayer 'Where is their God?' returns in Psalm 42:3 and 42:10 and Psalm 79:10, and the plea 'spare Your people' finds its answer in the very next unit. In the New Testament, the apostle Paul takes up the interior religion of verse 13 when he says that real circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, Romans 2:28 to 29. Jesus' words about fasting that is done in secret, Matthew 6:16 to 18, belong to the same tradition.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Joel wanted his hearers to hear two things at once and not let go of either. The first is that the situation is as grave as he has said: an army is on the way and the crisis is beyond human remedy. The second is that grave does not mean closed. The words 'yet even now' are the pastoral heart of the book. A prophet who had only judgment to announce could have stopped at verse 11. Joel instead spends the rest of the chapter showing that God's declared purpose is not to have the last word in judgment.

He also meant to correct a kind of religion that could survive any crisis because it lived at the surface. Torn clothes are a gesture that can be performed in an afternoon. Joel does not forbid the gesture, but he demotes it, and in doing so he asks his hearers to take the harder step, a changed direction of the whole person, 'with all your heart.' The longer list in verse 12, fasting, weeping and mourning, is meant to be the honest outward form of that inward return, not a substitute for it.

Finally, he meant the repentance to be corporate and public. The priests are given the very words of prayer to say. Leaders are not to wait for private spiritual feelings to bubble up from each person, but to lead a community into the presence of the God who has already declared His character. Joel's confidence rests on that character, and he wants his hearers to rest on it too.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This unit is largely prescriptive: it is a string of commands from God and from the prophet. The commands are tied, however, to a particular moment and to particular forms. Blowing the shofar in Zion, gathering at the temple court and having priests weep between the portico and the altar belong to Israel's covenant life under the old order. Believers today are not asked to reproduce the sanctuary arrangements, and the New Testament speaks of Christ as the one great High Priest, Hebrews 4:14 to 16.

What carries over is the pattern behind the forms. God invites rather than waiting to be bribed. Repentance is a whole-person turning, shown in what we do but located in the heart. It is both personal and shared, so that churches have good reason to confess and lament together. The ground of hope is always who God has revealed Himself to be, never the quality of our sorrow. A fast, where it is practised, is an expression of dependence, not a technique for forcing God's hand, and Jesus assumes that His followers will fast, in secret, Matthew 6:16 to 18.

One caution applies. Verse 14 describes a hope, not a guarantee of a particular outcome. It should not be read as promising that sincere repentance will always remove a given disaster in this life, nor as teaching that repentance purchases pardon. It teaches that those who turn are turning toward the God who has promised mercy.

debates.question: Does 'Who knows?' in verse 14 express doubt about God's forgiveness?

views.label: Humility before a free God
views.case: The phrase appears elsewhere when a person throws themselves on God's mercy without presuming to dictate terms. David uses it while his child is sick, 2 Samuel 12:22, and the king of Nineveh uses it in almost the same words as Joel, Jonah 3:9. It marks reverence for God's freedom, not distrust of His character, which verse 13 has just declared.

views.label: A real openness about the outcome
views.case: Others stress that the unsaid ending of the question is genuine. Even a penitent people cannot know what shape God's mercy will take or whether the immediate disaster will be lifted, because God is not bound to a formula. The 'may' guards against presuming on the covenant.

debates.bearing: Both readings keep repentance from becoming a transaction. They differ only on how much uncertainty remains. The next unit answers: God does spare, so the 'Who knows?' turns out to have been a door, not a wall.

debates.question: Can God 'relent' without changing, and what does verse 13 claim about Him?

views.label: God speaks in human terms and does not change
views.case: Texts like Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 say God is not a man that He should change His mind, and Malachi 3:6 says He does not change. On this view the language of relenting is how Scripture describes God's unchanging mercy toward people who stand in a new relation to Him once they repent. The disaster was always conditional, as Jeremiah 18:7 to 8 explains.

views.label: God truly responds in real time
views.case: Others take the language more literally. In Exodus 32:14, Jonah 3:10 and here God is portrayed as genuinely responding to His people's turning, so that the relationship has real give and take. His character, gracious and compassionate, stays constant, while His actions respond to what people do.

debates.bearing: Both agree on the point Joel presses: God's constant character is the reason repentance is worth attempting. They differ on how best to describe the way His mercy and His warnings interact, not on whether His mercy is real.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb shuv is the backbone of the passage, and it is worth following through the three verses. In verse 12 the people are told to shuv to God, in verse 13 they are told again, and in verse 14 God Himself is asked to shuv, to turn, in a verb that the BSB renders 'turn.' The English hides that it is the same word. The root carries the whole idea of coming home from exile in Deuteronomy 30:2, and it is the prophets' repeated call, Jeremiah 3:12 and Hosea 14:1. In Joel it is a pointed claim that repentance is relational: it is a change of direction towards a person. It is also the root of the verb used in the idiom for restoring fortunes, which appears in Joel 3:1.

The verb for tearing in verse 13, qara, is spelled almost the same as the verb for calling, qara, in Joel 2:32, although the two are distinct roots in Hebrew. The comparison is not an etymological point but it helps explain why a reader or hearer might feel the weight of the two commands together: tear what is closed, call what is near. Both 'hearts' and 'garments' are plural, so each person in the assembly is asked for a heart of his or her own.

The description in verse 13 is a quotation with adjustments. 'Gracious' translates channun, from the root for favour given freely, and 'compassionate' translates rachum, from the root that gives the word for womb, rechem, so that God's mercy is pictured as the tenderness a mother feels. 'Slow to anger' is literally 'long of nose,' erek appayim, the picture being of the long breath of patience as against the short, hot breath of rage. 'Abounding in loving devotion' is rav chesed, 'great in covenant love,' and the BSB's own footnote on the verse explains the range of chesed. Compared with Exodus 34:6, Joel reverses the order of the first two adjectives and ends not with truth but with 'relents from disaster.' In Hebrew that last verb is nicham, a stem that can mean to be sorry, to relent or to be comforted, used of God in Exodus 32:14 and Jonah 3:10.

The phrase 'leave a blessing behind Him' in verse 14 turns on the little word 'behind,' which pictures God walking away from the punishment and leaving a gift in His wake, where one would expect to find ruin. The words that follow explain the blessing: it is the restored ability to offer, which links to Joel 1:9.

Finally, in verse 17 the people are called God's 'heritage,' nachalah, the word used of Israel as the LORD's own possession, Deuteronomy 32:9. The prayer asks that this heritage not become a 'reproach,' cherpah, a word that will be taken up again in 2:19 where God promises never again to make them a cherpah among the nations. The prayer is answered in the same vocabulary it was asked in.

typology.type: The torn heart and the circumcised heart
typology.fulfillment: Joel sets an inward tearing against an outward one, and Deuteronomy 30:6 shows where the inward work comes from: God Himself circumcises the heart. Paul declares that real circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, Romans 2:29, and that believers were circumcised in Christ, Colossians 2:11. The correspondence is that what Joel commanded is what God supplies in the new covenant, Ezekiel 36:26 to 27. The type falls short in that Joel can only summon the people to a response, while in Christ the response is itself given.

typology.type: Priests weeping between the portico and the altar
typology.fulfillment: The priests stand where the sacrifices are laid and plead for the people. The picture of a mediator weeping for the people finds its fullness in Jesus, who wept over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41, and who 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near to God through Him, Hebrews 7:25. Unlike Joel's priests, He needs no sacrifice for Himself, Hebrews 7:27, and He has been tempted in every way, Hebrews 4:15. The type is incomplete because the priests could plead but could not themselves atone.

typology.type: 'Where is their God?' and the reproach among the nations
typology.fulfillment: The dread of Joel 2:17 is that God's people would become a laughing stock and God's name with them. That very mockery lands on Jesus. The crowd at the cross says, 'He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him,' Matthew 27:43, and Paul reads Psalm 69:9 as Christ taking on the reproaches of those who reproach God, Romans 15:3. Jesus' cry from the cross, Matthew 27:46, enters the experience of the silence behind the question. The correspondence is real, but the escalation is complete: the God who seemed absent was acting there to answer the question for every nation.

typology.type: The bridegroom called from his chamber
typology.fulfillment: Joel overrides the festival and the exemption of the newly married, because the crisis outranks the wedding. Jesus uses wedding imagery of Himself in Mark 2:19 to 20: the guests cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them, but the days will come when He is taken away and they will fast. In Him the wedding is the true feast, and the great wedding supper awaits, Revelation 19:7 to 9. Joel's picture of a joy suspended anticipates a joy that will not be suspended.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most plainly by way of its great problem. Joel commands a return with all the heart, and the command quietly shows that no one can supply what it asks. A torn heart cannot be made by tearing, any more than a clean heart can be washed by willpower. That is why the promise of Deuteronomy 30:6, that God will circumcise the heart, stands behind the command and why Ezekiel 36:26 to 27 and Jeremiah 31:33 later answer it with the promise of a new heart and the Spirit. The New Testament says that Christ is how those promises arrive: believers are given new birth, John 3:5 to 8, and 'the circumcision of Christ' is the setting aside of the old self, Colossians 2:11.

It leads to Christ as the answer to 'Who knows?' Joel's people could only hope that God might turn. In Christ the hope is grounded. The gracious and compassionate God of Exodus 34 sent the Son so that the justice that the word 'disaster' implied would be met without compromising mercy, Romans 3:25 to 26. The relenting of Joel is not that God discovers He was too hard on sinners but that a way is found by which He can be 'just and to justify,' Romans 3:26. When Paul writes that 'God's kindness leads you to repentance,' Romans 2:4, he is standing on verse 13.

It leads to Christ by the figure of the priest. The priests weep and pray the words they have been given, but the answer they seek rests on a mediator who can stand in the court and not need a sacrifice for himself. Hebrews presents Jesus as exactly that, a sympathetic high priest who can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, Hebrews 4:15 and 5:2. The weeping of Luke 19:41 is Joel's weeping brought to the city that did not know the time of its visitation.

It leads to Christ in the wedding. Joel interrupts a wedding with a fast, because the Day makes everything else small. Jesus enters the world as the bridegroom, and the guests cannot fast while He is with them, Mark 2:19 to 20. The time of fasting returns when He is taken away, which His followers did, and will, until the wedding supper of the Lamb.

A note of restraint. Joel's own hearers were not looking at a crucified Messiah when they heard these words, and the text does not say that the 'blessing behind Him' is Christ. The link is made by the shape of the promise and by the New Testament's own use of Joel's themes: a God who asks for the heart is a God who supplies it, and He does so in His Son. The passage points to Christ by the pattern, then, rather than by hidden code, and it points with a clarity the later texts confirm.
study.god:
The passage rests on a single sentence, verse 13, and every other attribute of God in the passage hangs on it. God describes Himself in five terms that run in a deliberate sequence: gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, relenting from disaster. They begin with the kindness that gives what is not earned and end in the action that stops the harm that is deserved. That sequence is the moral logic of the passage. God's patience and loyalty are not abstract qualities but the ground of an actual change of course.

God here is the one who speaks first. The invitation of verse 12 is from the LORD in the first person, 'declares the LORD,' and it comes before any sign that anyone has repented. This overturns the idea that God waits for people to climb partway and then responds. The God of Joel breaks into a collapsing situation and says 'yet even now.' His initiative is also what makes the human response possible.

God is free. 'Who knows?' is not doubt about His character but acknowledgement that He cannot be managed. He is not bound by the people's tears, and His mercy cannot be demanded as a debt. That freedom is not capriciousness; verse 13 says what He is like. It is the freedom of a gracious person who may give more than was asked, or give differently, and so mercy remains mercy.

God is the one who cares about the heart over the display. He does not scorn the outward signs, for He commands the fast and the weeping in verse 12, but He refuses to be content with them. A God who looks on the heart cannot be fooled by theatre, and this is a comfort as well as a challenge, because it means that sincere turning is known and welcomed even when it is clumsy.

God is concerned for His name among the nations. The priests' prayer in verse 17 gives two grounds for pity: the people are His heritage, and the nations will ask, 'Where is their God?' The LORD's reputation is bound to the fate of His people, which is why His deliverance of them is never merely a private favour but a witness to the world.

For worship, the passage teaches us to come in boldness without arrogance. We may approach because He has told us who He is, and we should approach with whole hearts because He is not to be treated casually. The two together, confidence and reverence, are the temper of true prayer: 'return to the LORD your God,' who is, in the same breath, gracious and compassionate.

crossReferences.note: The source of the creed in verse 13. After the golden calf, God answered Moses' request to see His glory by proclaiming His name. Joel quotes the first half, the mercy, and does not need to quote the second half about visiting guilt, because he applies the first to a people returning. Compare the order of the adjectives and the closing phrase in the two passages.

Nineveh's king says, 'Who knows? God may turn and relent,' using almost Joel's words, and God does relent. A pagan city shows that Joel's hope was not naive, and Jonah 4:2 quotes the same creed as the reason God spared them. The two books read together show how wide the door of repentance stands.

Moses foresaw a people scattered by judgment who would return to the LORD with all their heart and soul, and then he promised that God would circumcise their hearts. Joel's command to return with all the heart stands inside this promise, and shows that the hope depends on God's work in the heart as much as on the people's turning.

Isaiah shows how a fast can become a performance, bowing the head like a reed while oppression goes on. The true fast loosens the chains of injustice. Together with Joel, it shows that the outward act is acceptable only when the heart and the life match it, and that prophets treat sincerity as the point of fasting.

David says that God does not delight in sacrifice but that a broken spirit and a broken and contrite heart He will not despise. The psalm is the prayer of a man who has done what Joel asks, and it shows what rending the heart looks like in a person. It also shows that the offerings returned to the altar only after the heart was right, Psalm 51:19.

The earlier call to fasting uses the same words as verse 15, consecrate a fast, proclaim a sacred assembly. Back then the priests were told to lament in sackcloth. Reading the two calls side by side shows that the first call was a response to the plague, while the second call is a response to the invitation of God, and it comes with a ground of hope.

Hosea's own call to return mixes sincere hope with the shallow certainty that God will heal quickly, and God's own reply in verse 4 shows that He was not impressed. Placed beside Joel it clarifies the difference between presuming on mercy and humbly seeking it. Joel's 'Who knows?' is the humbler posture.

The psalmist prays for help for the glory of God's name and asks why the nations should say 'Where is their God?' The prayer that Joel puts into the priests' mouths belongs to a recognisable tradition of petition that grounds a request in the honour of God, not in the merit of those who ask.

The younger son 'came to his senses' and began the walk home with a prepared speech, and while he was still far off the father ran to meet him. The story shows the shape of Joel's call and God's response: the return is real and humble, and the welcome comes before the speech is finished.

God promises to remove the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh, and to put His Spirit within. Joel's command to tear the heart is the demand, and this passage is the supply. It also leads directly into Joel 2:28 to 29, where the Spirit is promised, which is the next step in the book.

Jesus assumes His followers will fast and tells them to do it in secret, not to be seen by others. This is Joel's priority, inward before outward, restated by the one who is the final authority on what the Father sees. The Father who sees in secret is the God of Joel 2:13 who looks on the heart.

study.oneStory:
This passage sits at the point in the Bible's story where the question of what a righteous God does with a guilty people is asked most directly, and where the answer is first given in the form that every later generation would cling to. Joel did not invent that answer. It was given at Sinai, Exodus 34:6 to 7, in the moment the covenant seemed shattered by the golden calf, and Joel repeats it in a new emergency. The thread from the fall to the golden calf to the locust plague is the same: people turn from God, judgment falls, and God's first word after the judgment is an invitation.

What the passage answers from earlier in the story is the long problem of a covenant people who keep breaking the covenant. Deuteronomy had already said that exile would not be the end, that a return with the whole heart would find compassion, and that God would one day circumcise the heart. Joel hears that promise in the middle of a plague and tells the people it applies now. The command to return is the old promise made urgent.

What the passage sets up is the dual movement that the rest of the book, and the Bible, will follow. The assembly gathered here is the first of a series of gatherings that culminate in the great gathering of the nations in chapter 3 and the gathering of every tribe and language in Revelation 7:9. The torn heart looks ahead to the new heart, the Spirit promised in Joel 2:28, and the new covenant of Jeremiah 31. The priests' prayer, 'spare Your people,' looks ahead to the One who stands between God and the people with the authority to secure their sparing, Hebrews 7:25.

It also sets up the hardest question the Bible faces: how can God relent from disaster without ceasing to be just? Joel states the mercy and leaves the mechanism unspoken. The answer unfolds across Scripture and arrives at the cross, where God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice, so as to be 'just and to justify,' Romans 3:25 to 26. The gracious and compassionate God of Joel 2:13 acts there, and what He relents from is carried by His Son.

In the new creation the passage's questions are all answered. No one asks 'Where is their God?' because 'God Himself will be with them as their God,' Revelation 21:3. The fast gives way to the wedding supper, Revelation 19:9, and the grief for which the garments were once torn is wiped away, Revelation 21:4. The call to return becomes the open invitation of Revelation 22:17, where the Spirit and the bride say 'Come,' and God's own character, first named at Sinai, turns out to have been the truth about the universe all along.

sermon.why: No expository sermon on Joel 2:12-17 from a trusted expositor could be verified by web search this session; a passage-level exposition can be added later once confirmed.

quiz.q: What does the phrase 'yet even now' signal in the book of Joel?

options.text: The turning point where God opens the door of mercy despite the looming judgment.
options.note: It pivots the book from terror to the invitation to return.

options.text: A final warning that the time for repentance has already passed.
options.note: The opposite: it declares the door is still open.

options.text: A shift in tone toward hope, even while judgment still looms.
options.note: It does shift toward hope, specifically by inviting repentance.

options.text: A statement that God has changed His mind and will never judge.
options.note: God still calls for repentance; mercy is offered to those who return.

quiz.q: What does 'rend your hearts and not your garments' teach about repentance?

options.text: True repentance is inward and whole-hearted, not merely an outward show of grief.
options.note: God wants the heart broken, not just the clothes torn.

options.text: Outward signs of mourning are forbidden and always wrong.
options.note: The point is not that outward signs are banned, but that they must not replace the heart.

options.text: Sincere sorrow should reach deeper than external rituals.
options.note: Right emphasis, though Joel specifically contrasts heart with garments.

options.text: Repentance is only about feelings and never involves any action.
options.note: Joel still calls for fasting, assembly, and turning; the heart drives the actions.

quiz.q: On what basis does Joel ground the call to return?

options.text: On God's revealed character: gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in love.
options.note: Verse 13 quotes Exodus 34, resting hope on who God is.

options.text: On the people's track record of faithfulness.
options.note: The ground is God's character, not the people's merit.

options.text: On the promise that God relents from disaster for those who turn back.
options.note: True, and that relenting flows from His gracious character named in the verse.

options.text: On the fear that God is harsh and must be appeased with ritual.
options.note: The appeal is to God's grace, not to appeasing a harsh deity.

quiz.q: How do the pleading priests point forward to Christ?

options.text: They foreshadow Jesus, the great High Priest who intercedes and secures the sparing He asks for.
options.note: Christ both pleads for His people and provides what the plea requires.

options.text: They show that only human priests can ever stand between God and people.
options.note: Their ministry points beyond itself to the one true Priest, Jesus.

options.text: They model intercession that Christ perfects and fulfills.
options.note: True, and Christ not only models but accomplishes the sparing by His sacrifice.

options.text: They prove that intercession is pointless before God.
options.note: Their intercession is honored and finds its fulfillment in Christ's.

quiz.q: What does 'Who knows? He may turn and relent' express?

options.text: Reverent humility before God's freedom, not doubt about His gracious character.
options.note: It guards against treating repentance as a lever to control God.

options.text: That forgiveness is a gamble God might refuse on a whim.
options.note: God's mercy toward the penitent is sure; the humility concerns His sovereign freedom.

options.text: Genuine hope that leaves the specific outcome in God's sovereign hands.
options.note: True, held together with the certainty of His gracious character in verse 13.

options.text: That God is unpredictable and cannot be trusted at all.
options.note: The whole appeal rests on trusting God's revealed graciousness.

questions: God breaks in with 'yet even now.' Is there a sin or a season you have written off as too late for God to redeem? How does His invitation speak to that?
Joel calls for torn hearts, not just torn clothes. Where might your repentance be staying at the level of appearances rather than reaching the heart?
The hope of this passage rests on who God is, not on how well we perform. How does grounding your repentance in God's gracious character change the way you come to Him?
The whole community, from nursing infants to elders, was summoned to seek God together. What would whole-hearted corporate repentance look like in your church or family?
Only Christ can give the new heart this passage exposes our need for. Where do you need to stop trying to fix your own heart and ask Him to renew it?

translationNotes.note: This verse quotes the self-revelation of God in Exodus 34:6. BSB footnotes that the Hebrew chesed, rendered 'loving devotion,' spans love, kindness, faithfulness, mercy, and covenant loyalty.
'He relents from sending disaster' renders the Hebrew nicham; it describes God being moved to spare the penitent, not a change in His character or a mistake corrected.
'Who knows?' expresses reverent hope rather than doubt, guarding repentance from becoming a mechanism to compel God while still expecting His mercy.
